core: The broad lower-case label classical music as Western art music in an introductory course context
The distinction between broad classical music and the capitalized Classical Period of roughly 1750–1820s
Listening through musical elements, genres, performing forces, and historical context
supporting: A broad chronological map from medieval music through contemporary work without treating period boundaries as exact walls
Common Classical Period genres such as the symphony, sonata, and string quartet
Limits of canon-based labels and claims of inherent hierarchy
outOfScope: A complete history of Western art music or biographies of individual composers
Detailed theory, score analysis, or period-style performance practice
Claims that Western classical music is universal, more sophisticated, or superior to other musical traditions
Using a single composer, era, or national tradition as representative of all classical music

claims.claim: In the cited LOUIS course context, lower-case classical music is a broad label for Western art music from about 900 CE to the present, while the Classical Period is a more specific historical era of roughly 1750–1820s.

The LOUIS Music Appreciation book organizes its Western-music history coverage through medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical Period, nineteenth-century or Romantic, and twentieth- and twenty-first-century chapters, showing that the broad label covers more than the Classical Period alone.
The cited Classical Period chapter associates that particular era with balance and symmetry and identifies instrumental genres including the symphony, sonata, and string quartet.
The same source describes public concerts devoted to instrumental genres as an important development of the Classical Period, rather than a universal description of all music called classical.

Classical music can be approached through specific audible evidence in melody, rhythm, harmony, texture, timbre, dynamics, form, and performing forces rather than through period labels or composer reputation alone.
The broad label is useful for an introductory course but should be scoped to its historical and cultural context rather than used as a universal measure of musical value or complexity.
